findings.title: SQL injection — the unvalidated `tables` array is interpolated into raw Neon SQL in POST /api/backup
findings.evidence: app/api/backup/route.ts:26-39 declares `tables?: string[]` in the request body and passes it straight through with no validation: `const payload = await exportBackup(userId, email, { tables: body?.tables })`. lib/backup.ts:187 then does `const tables = opts.tables && opts.tables.length > 0 ? opts.tables : [...BACKUP_TABLES]`, and lib/backup.ts:31 executes `(sql as any).unsafe(`select * from public.${table} where ${keyCol} = $1`, [userId])` — the table name is string-interpolated into a raw, non-parameterised statement. Contrast app/api/backup/csv/[table]/route.ts:13, which DOES allowlist: `if (!table || !(BACKUP_TABLES as readonly string[]).includes(table))`.
findings.impact: Any authenticated landlord can inject arbitrary SQL into a raw Neon statement and read the rows back — the payload is echoed in the response at app/api/backup/route.ts:92. That is cross-tenant exfiltration of every table in the database (other landlords' properties, tenants, payments, user_profiles) plus whatever write/DDL the Neon role may perform. The `withAuth` same-origin check is not a barrier: the attacker simply sets `Origin: <host>` on the request.
findings.fix: Validate `body.tables` with `z.array(z.enum(BACKUP_TABLES))` in the route, and make lib/backup.ts refuse any table that is not in the allowlist before it reaches a query. Never build a statement by interpolating an identifier — map a validated name to a hard-coded statement.
findings.fix_notes: app/api/backup/route.ts validates the caller-supplied tables array with assertAllowedBackupTable() and returns 400 on the first invalid entry. lib/backup.ts validates again internally (defence in depth) and exportBackup() validates every table up front.

findings.title: SQL injection — attacker-controlled column names in the backup/restore INSERT builder
findings.evidence: lib/backup.ts:59 builds the column list by string-concatenating the restored row's keys: `insert into public.${table} (${Object.keys(safe).map((k) => `"${k}"`).join(",")}) values (...)`. Those keys come straight from the request body: lib/system.ts:118 declares `data: z.record(z.string(), z.array(z.record(z.any())))`, which puts no constraint on key names, and lib/system.ts:145 `sanitiseRow()` only strips a fixed NEVER_BACKUP list of key names — it never validates them. A key containing `"` terminates the quoted identifier and injects arbitrary SQL text. The `on conflict (id) do update set "${k}" = $n` branch (lib/backup.ts:71 and :83) repeats the same key at a second injection point.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can execute attacker-chosen SQL against the live database by POSTing a crafted backup payload to /api/backup/import — a full read/write exfiltration primitive. The table is allowlisted and `user_id` is re-stamped (lib/backup.ts:55) so the table is safe; the columns are not.
findings.fix: Resolve every row's keys against a per-table column allowlist derived from the schema and reject unknown keys before any SQL is built; at minimum enforce /^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$/ on every key. Apply the validation to the skip, replace and merge branches.
findings.fix_notes: lib/backup.ts builds every restore statement through buildRestoreInsert(), which rejects unsafe or unknown column names BEFORE producing any SQL, and binds values as parameters. All three insert branches covered.

findings.title: MIGRATION_SECRET / CRON_SECRET / BACKUP_CRON_SECRET are required but compared with `===`, not in constant time
findings.evidence: `if (expected && got === expected) return null` and `if (got !== secret) { return errorResponse("Forbidden: missing or invalid CRON_SECRET", 403) }`. The same codebase gets it right elsewhere: app/api/mpesa/callback/route.ts:34 uses `timingSafeEqual` with a length guard. The secrets themselves ARE genuinely required, not merely mentioned in a comment — each route returns 503 in production when the env var is unset (app/api/migrations/run/route.ts:36-47, app/api/cron/run/route.ts:23-25, app/api/backup/auto/route.ts:28-36) — and all of them are read from headers (`x-migration-secret`, `x-cron-secret`, `Authorization: Bearer`), never from a query string; a repository-wide search for `searchParams.get("secret")` returns nothing.
findings.impact: A timing side channel on the only barrier between the internet and the migration/cron/backup-admin endpoints. The correct pattern already exists in the codebase but was not applied to these five sites, so the inconsistency is likely to be regressed by future edits.
findings.fix: Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` with a byte-length pre-check on all five comparisons, matching app/api/mpesa/callback/route.ts:34.
findings.fix_notes: New lib/api/secure-compare.ts exports timingSafeEqualString() (crypto.timingSafeEqual with an equal-length guard). Used by migrations/run, migrations/reset, migrations/rollback (MIGRATION_SECRET), cron/run (CRON_SECRET) and backup/auto (BACKUP_CRON_SECRET). Fail-closed semantics unchanged.

findings.title: M-Pesa C2B confirmation/validation authenticate only by an IP allowlist that fails open when unset
findings.evidence: The only gate is `if (!isFromSafaricom(request.headers.get("x-forwarded-for"))) { return NextResponse.json({ ResultCode: 1, ResultDesc: "Forbidden" }, { status: 403 }) }` on a route documented as `Public endpoint, no auth (Daraja can't authenticate)` (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:19). lib/mpesa/daraja.ts:268-272: `const list = (process.env.MPESA_ALLOWED_CALLBACK_IPS || "").split(",").map((s) => s.trim()).filter(Boolean); if (list.length === 0) { return process.env.MPESA_ENV !== "production" }`. `MPESA_ENV` defaults to sandbox (lib/mpesa/daraja.ts:47), so an unset allowlist plus a non-production MPESA_ENV means every IP is accepted. On success the handler inserts a `rent_payments` row with `status: 'paid'` (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:185-193) and increments the paybill counters.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated payment mutation: anyone can POST a forged Daraja confirmation and mark a rent payment paid without any money moving. Today the middleware masks this — lib/supabase/middleware.ts:55-58 does not list /api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation in `isExternalApi`, so middleware.ts:82-87 401s the request and real Daraja callbacks also fail. The obvious fix (adding the path to the allowlist) instantly exposes the fail-open guard.
findings.fix: Require a shared secret header (reuse MPESA_CALLBACK_SECRET and the existing timing-safe compare) on the C2B endpoints; make the allowlist fail closed when unset in production; derive the client IP from the platform-controlled header (`x-vercel-forwarded-for`) rather than the first `x-forwarded-for` hop; add the C2B paths to the middleware allowlist in the same change.
findings.fix_notes: The C2B allowlist now fails CLOSED: an unset or empty MPESA_ALLOWED_CALLBACK_IPS rejects the callback instead of allowing everything. The shared secret MPESA_CALLBACK_SECRET is accepted as a second factor (constant-time compare). The client address comes only from a platform-overwritten header (x-vercel-forwarded-for, cf-connecting-ip, x-real-ip) — x-forwarded-for is never read for an authorisation decision. lib/supabase/middleware.ts was updated in the same pass so the two C2B paths can actually reach the route — safe now precisely because the allowlist and the secret fail closed. Regression tests in lib/mpesa/mpesa-routes.security.test.ts.

findings.title: M-Pesa STK callback allowlist reads the client-controllable first x-forwarded-for hop
findings.evidence: `const forwardedFor = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0].trim() || null` followed by `if (!isFromSafaricom(forwardedFor)) { return NextResponse.json({ ResultCode: 1, ResultDesc: "Rejected" }, { status: 403 }) }`. The XFF convention is client-first — the first entry is the value the client sent and intermediaries append to it. The route does also accept MPESA_CALLBACK_SECRET compared with `timingSafeEqual` (line 34), which is the correct primary control, but the IP check is presented as a second factor.
findings.impact: The documented IP allowlist (MPESA_ALLOWED_CALLBACK_IPS) is bypassable by sending `X-Forwarded-For: <safaricom-ip>`. Any deployment that relies on the IP allowlist rather than the secret loses the control entirely.
findings.fix: Use the platform-set header (`x-vercel-forwarded-for`) or the last XFF entry, not the first; keep MPESA_CALLBACK_SECRET as the mandatory primary control and treat the IP list as defence-in-depth only.
findings.fix_notes: The allowlist is now evaluated against the platform-set client address only — x-vercel-forwarded-for, cf-connecting-ip or x-real-ip (lib/mpesa/daraja.ts TRUSTED_IP_HEADERS). x-forwarded-for is not consulted at all, so a forged header cannot satisfy the check.

findings.title: M-Pesa callback marks the invoice paid without comparing the settled amount to the invoice
findings.evidence: The callback metadata contains `Amount` (documented at line 16) but the handler only reads `meta.MpesaReceiptNumber` and `meta.TransactionDate` (lines 73-74). It then runs `.from("rent_payments").update({ status: "paid", paid_date: ..., payment_method: "mpesa", reference_number: ... }).eq("id", tx.payment_id).eq("user_id", tx.user_id)` (lines 92-103) with no comparison against `tx.amount` — the amount column is selected on line 82 and then never used. Upstream, app/api/mpesa/stkpush/route.ts:17-22 accepts any positive `amount` from the client and never compares it with the tenant's `monthly_rent` (selected on line 37).
findings.impact: A KES 1 payment settles a KES 250,000 rent invoice: neither the push nor the callback enforces that the money that arrived equals the money that was owed. The rent ledger, arrears figures and landlord revenue reports are therefore untrustworthy.
findings.fix: Derive the expected amount server-side from the rent invoice, reject a push whose amount does not match it, and in the callback compare `Number(meta.Amount)` with `tx.amount` (tolerance ±1 KES) before flipping the row to `paid`; mark mismatches `unmatched` for review instead.
findings.fix_notes: The callback now compares the settled amount against both the charged amount and the rent invoice before an invoice is marked paid, with an explicit, documented rounding tolerance. A mismatch leaves the invoice unpaid and is recorded for review.

findings.title: A paid subscription is granted for free when MPESA_ENV is not `production` or MPESA_SANDBOX_MOCK=1
findings.evidence: `const env = (process.env.MPESA_ENV === "production" ? "production" : "sandbox")` (line 47) — the default is sandbox. In mock mode `stkQuery()` returns a hard-coded success (`ResponseCode: "0"`, `ResultCode: "0"`, lines 203-212) and `stkPush()` returns a synthetic success (lines 143-151). app/api/subscription/checkout-status/route.ts:32-33 turns that into `completed = true`, and lines 55-79 then upsert `subscriptions` with `status: "active"` and `current_period_end: now + 30 days`. The only guard on the push side is `if (!darajaConfigured() && process.env.MPESA_SANDBOX_MOCK !== "1")` (app/api/subscription/checkout/route.ts:37) — i.e. mock mode explicitly disables the guard.
findings.impact: A production deployment that leaves MPESA_ENV at its default, or sets MPESA_SANDBOX_MOCK=1 (a value present in local .env files and easy to copy into the dashboard), self-approves every payment. The user receives a real, active, paid subscription for free. This is precisely the 'invoice marked paid without money moving' scenario.
findings.fix: Refuse to run any payment path unless MPESA_ENV === "production" AND MPESA_SANDBOX_MOCK !== "1"; make the mock path unreachable in production (fail closed at startup); never derive a paid entitlement from a status query the client can trigger.
findings.fix_notes: The library can no longer be tricked into a mock payment: MPESA_ENV selects the Daraja sandbox only when it is exactly "sandbox" (unset, blank or a typo all mean production), and the mock transport additionally requires NODE_ENV to be development or test, so a self-hosted production box cannot self-approve a payment. The entitlement decision lives in app/api/subscription/checkout-status/route.ts, which now REFUSES a mocked Daraja result outright and, in a production runtime, refuses any result that did not come from the production gateway.

findings.title: Two disagreeing sources of truth for 'is this route public?' — the middleware allowlist vs per-route withAuth
findings.evidence: The middleware 401s every anonymous /api/** request except exactly three hard-coded paths: `pathname === "/api/health" || pathname === "/api/cron/run" || pathname === "/api/mpesa/callback"`. Meanwhile ~20 route files are written as public-by-design and contain no auth check of their own: app/api/contact/route.ts:23, app/api/newsletter/route.ts:17, app/api/pricing/lead/route.ts:19, app/api/enterprise/lead/route.ts:21, app/api/feedback/route.ts:16, app/api/customer-requests/route.ts:37, app/api/geocode/route.ts:3, app/api/blog, /api/docs, /api/features, /api/solutions, /api/roadmap, /api/plans, /api/brand, /api/templates, app/api/backup/auto/route.ts:126 (GET), app/api/system/ping/route.ts:12, app/api/system/version/route.ts:11, app/api/system/patches/route.ts:11, app/api/system/patches/check/route.ts:13. The error runs both ways: /api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation is documented as public (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:19) but is 401'd by the middleware, so genuine Daraja callbacks cannot land.
findings.impact: The effective auth posture of ~94 routes is decided by a 3-line string list in a different file from the route logic. A new public route is one matcher change away from being exposed, and a public route that looks protected in the middleware is in fact broken.
findings.fix: Have each route declare its own posture explicitly (e.g. `export const access = "public"`), enforce it in one place, and delete the parallel allowlist in the middleware. At minimum add an integration test that asserts the intended posture of every route.

findings.title: System endpoints leak infrastructure metadata to anonymous callers
findings.evidence: `/api/system/ping` returns `{ ok, db: "neon" | "supabase", latency_ms, schema_version, timestamp }` (lines 36-44). `/api/system/version` returns `{ app: { name, version, commit }, schema: { current }, node: process.version }`. `/api/system/patches/check` returns the patches that have NOT been applied to production (`pending`) — a live map of the schema drift on the real database. `/api/backup/auto` GET returns `opted_in_users` (a count of the user base) and the latest scheduled backup. None of them require a session or a secret; they are protected only by the middleware catch-all (see INFRA-008).
findings.impact: Reconnaissance material: the database provider, the exact schema version, the Node runtime, the deployed git commit, how many landlords use the product, and which schema patches are missing on production — which tells an attacker which security controls have not been applied.
findings.fix: Keep only `{ ok: true }` on a genuinely public probe; move version/patch/ping detail behind withAuth or a dedicated ops secret, and drop the pending-patch list from any non-operator response.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy anywhere in the app
findings.evidence: The `headers()` block for `source: "/(.*)"` sets exactly five headers: `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000`, `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`, `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`. There is no `Content-Security-Policy` and no `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`.
findings.impact: No allow-list in front of script execution, no `object-src 'none'`, no `base-uri`, no `frame-ancestors`, and no reporting channel. A single injection anywhere in the app executes with the full privileges of the page — and because the marketing site and the dashboard share one origin, that includes the dashboard's session.
findings.fix: Ship `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-<per-request>'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; img-src 'self' data: https://*.supabase.co; connect-src 'self' https://*.supabase.co` with a report endpoint, collect violations, then flip to enforced.
findings.fix_notes: A Content-Security-Policy now ships as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only. It is deliberately not enforcing: an enforcing policy without a per-request nonce would break Next inline bootstrap scripts. The exact header value and the switch-over procedure are in audit/deliverable-storage-infra.md section 6.

findings.title: Missing cross-origin / HSTS / Permissions-Policy hardening headers
findings.evidence: Present: `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (a good value), `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000`, `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`, `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`. Absent: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy`, `Content-Security-Policy` (see INFRA-010), `X-XSS-Protection` (or an explicit `0` to retire the legacy filter), `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy`. The HSTS value carries neither `includeSubDomains` nor `preload`. Permissions-Policy omits `payment`, `usb`, `accelerometer`, `gyroscope` and `interest-cohort`.
findings.impact: `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` alone is the legacy clickjacking control; `frame-ancestors` in a CSP is the modern equivalent and is missing. HSTS without `includeSubDomains` leaves every subdomain (staging, preview, *.vercel.app) willing to serve plaintext on a first visit, so a subdomain takeover can be used to strip the flag. COOP/CORP absent means the app can be framed and its responses embedded cross-origin.
findings.fix: Add `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin` (or `cross-origin` for the storage host), `X-XSS-Protection: 0`, `frame-ancestors 'none'` via CSP, extend HSTS to `max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`, and complete the Permissions-Policy list.
findings.fix_notes: The HSTS header is now max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload. COOP and CORP were deliberately NOT added: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin can break the Supabase/Google OAuth popup flow, and Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy needs per-route thought because images are served from Supabase.

findings.title: No rate limiting on any endpoint, including auth, password reset, public forms and M-Pesa push
findings.lines: 11-50 (signIn), 56-107 (signUp); app/(marketing)/auth/forgot-password/action.ts:5-15; app/api/contact/route.ts:23; app/api/newsletter/route.ts:17; app/api/pricing/lead/route.ts:19; app/api/enterprise/lead/route.ts:21; app/api/feedback/route.ts:16; app/api/customer-requests/route.ts:37; app/api/mpesa/stkpush/route.ts:12; app/api/subscription/checkout/route.ts:16; app/api/templates/[id]/docx/route.ts:12; app/api/geocode/route.ts:3
findings.evidence: A repository-wide search for a rate limiter returns nothing in application code — only marketing copy (lib/content/marketing.ts:551) and a changelog claim. `signIn()` calls `supabase.auth.signInWithPassword` with no per-IP or per-account throttle; `requestPasswordReset()` calls `supabase.auth.resetPasswordForEmail` with no throttle; the lead/contact/newsletter/feedback endpoints accept and log a submission on every request. The only throttling in existence is Supabase's own email rate limit, which lib/actions.ts:86 merely surfaces as an error message. The changelog entry at lib/content/site.ts:69-72 claims 'Added per-IP rate limiting on /auth/login and a tamper-evident audit log for sensitive actions' — neither exists in this code.
findings.impact: Credential stuffing and password-reset email bombing against the auth endpoint; unlimited spam into the lead/contact/newsletter inboxes (each submission is also console.info'd server-side — a log-volume DoS); an attacker can flood the Daraja STK-push endpoint, burn the merchant's Safaricom quota and generate real payment prompts to arbitrary MSISDNs; `POST /api/templates/[id]/docx` is unbounded CPU-bound document generation; `GET /api/geocode` is an unthrottled relay to Nominatim whose usage policy will get the app's egress IP banned.
findings.fix: Add a shared rate limiter (Vercel KV / Upstash Redis) keyed by IP + user + route, and apply it to: the auth actions (login / sign-up / reset), every public marketing form, STK push + checkout, docx rendering, and the geocode relay. Return 429 with Retry-After. Also correct the false changelog claim at lib/content/site.ts:69-72.

findings.title: Documents and property photos live in a PUBLIC Supabase Storage bucket — the storage RLS policies are not a control
findings.evidence: `INSERT INTO storage.buckets (id, name, public) VALUES ('documents', 'documents', true)` — the bucket is public. The file states the intent: `-- The bucket is public-readable so the app can render the URL directly without a signed-URL round-trip. Files are still scoped per-user via the path prefix (userId/...) enforced by the policies above.` (lines 353-355). For a public bucket the `storage.objects` SELECT policies (lines 340-343) do not protect the public object endpoint — any holder of the URL gets the bytes. app/api/documents/upload/route.ts:48 then hands the client `supabase.storage.from("documents").getPublicUrl(path)`, and app/api/properties/[id]/photos/route.ts:70 does the same for photos.
findings.impact: Every lease agreement, contract, ID scan, invoice and property photo is permanently world-readable at a stable URL. There is no expiry, no revocation and no access log. The object path is `{userId}/{Date.now()}-{filename}` — the user UUID is the only barrier, and user IDs are returned by numerous APIs and appear in URLs, emails and logs. One leaked link (a referrer, a proxy log, a shared chat message, a support screenshot) is permanent unauthenticated access to a landlord's confidential documents. Property photos share the same bucket and the same public path.
findings.fix: Make the bucket private, persist `storage_path` instead of `file_url`, and serve objects through short-lived signed URLs — the codebase already has the pattern in lib/storage.ts:59-68 (`getBackupSignedUrl`, 600 s). Serve downloads with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and migrate the existing objects.
findings.fix_notes: The documents bucket is created private (ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET public = false, so re-running the SQL flips an existing bucket too), with owner-scoped USING and WITH CHECK policies that are now meaningful for reads. Every read goes through a 5-minute signed URL bound to the requesting owner. file_url now stores the Storage object path.

findings.title: /api/documents/upload validates neither content type nor magic bytes and stores the client-declared MIME type
findings.evidence: The only checks are `if (!(file instanceof File))` and `if (file.size > 10 * 1024 * 1024)`. The upload then uses `contentType: file.type || "application/octet-stream"` (line 37) — `file.type` is the content type the client sent in the multipart part, i.e. attacker-controlled — with no extension allowlist and no magic-byte sniff. The filename is sanitised correctly (`file.name.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9._-]/g, "_")`, line 29) so path traversal is not possible, but the type is unconstrained. The error message on line 43 even instructs the operator to make the bucket public.
findings.impact: An authenticated user can upload arbitrary content — HTML, script-bearing SVG, a polyglot — into a bucket that is publicly readable (INFRA-013) and is served with the attacker-chosen content type. The app's `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` applies to the app's own origin (next.config.mjs:32) but not to the Supabase storage origin, so the browser may render the uploaded file as HTML from the storage host: a stored-XSS primitive on the storage domain and a ready-made malware/phishing host.
findings.fix: Allowlist extensions and content types, verify the magic bytes of the file's first bytes, derive the stored content type from the sniffed type rather than the client's claim, and serve downloads with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `nosniff`.
findings.fix_notes: Content-type allowlist, extension allowlist, magic-byte sniff, 10 MB limit and filename sanitisation are implemented, and the upload now uses the user-scoped client. NOT DONE: serving the file with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

findings.title: Property photo upload trusts the client-declared MIME type and writes through the service-role key
findings.evidence: `if (!ALLOWED.has(file.type)) throw new HttpError("Image must be PNG/JPEG/WEBP/GIF", 415)` — `file.type` is the client-declared multipart content type and the file's actual bytes are never inspected. The storage client is chosen as `const storageClient = serviceKey && url ? createServiceClient(url, serviceKey, { auth: { persistSession: false } }) : supabase` (lines 59-63), i.e. the service-role key, which bypasses the `storage.objects` INSERT policy at supabase-setup/01-create-tables.sql:336-339 that is supposed to scope writes to the caller's own folder. The object is written into the shared `documents` bucket at `property-photos/${userId}/${params.id}/${randomUUID()}.${ext}`.
findings.impact: Two problems. (1) Any non-image bytes are accepted as long as the client says `image/png`, and the file is then served from the public bucket with a client-controlled content type. (2) Because the write uses the service role, the per-user storage policy is never exercised — the storage layer is not a control on this path, which is exactly the control the schema claims to provide.
findings.fix: Sniff the magic bytes (PNG `89 50 4E 47`, JPEG `FF D8 FF`, GIF `47 49 46`, WEBP `RIFF....WEBP`) and re-encode with sharp; upload with the caller's own scoped client so the storage policy applies; keep the bucket private (INFRA-013).
findings.fix_notes: The magic-byte sniff is implemented, the upload now uses the user-scoped Supabase client instead of the service key, and the property ownership is verified BEFORE the upload. NOT DONE: re-encoding the image through sharp — no sharp dependency, and it was out of scope.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER RPCs executable by `anon`/`authenticated` allow cross-tenant tampering and deletion
findings.evidence: `create or replace function public.bump_paybill_counters(p_paybill_id uuid, p_matched boolean) returns void language sql security definer as $$ update public.paybills set matched_count = ... where id = p_paybill_id; $$;` followed by `grant execute on function public.bump_paybill_counters(uuid, boolean) to service_role, anon, authenticated;` — the function updates `public.paybills` for ANY paybill id, never checks the caller, and does not pin `search_path`. `supabase-setup/12-auto-backup.sql:11-32` defines `prune_old_backups()` the same way (security definer, no `set search_path`) and grants `execute ... to service_role, authenticated`; it deletes every `backups` row beyond each user's 50 most recent — for all users.
findings.impact: Any anonymous internet caller can `POST https://<project>.supabase.co/rest/v1/rpc/bump_paybill_counters` with an arbitrary paybill UUID and inflate `matched_count` / `unmatched_count` and set `last_payment_at` on a landlord's paybill — the counters the dashboard presents as payments received. Any registered user can call `prune_old_backups()` and destroy other tenants' backup history. Neither function pins `search_path`, so both are also exposed to search_path hijacking.
findings.fix: `revoke execute ... from anon, authenticated;` and grant only to `service_role`; add `set search_path = public, pg_temp;` to both bodies; call them from the internal routes with the service-role client instead of exposing them as RPCs.
findings.fix_notes: REVOKE EXECUTE FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated + GRANT EXECUTE TO service_role on both SECURITY DEFINER functions, and both now pin SET search_path = public, pg_temp. Function bodies are unchanged.

findings.title: The Supabase fallback instructs the operator to create an arbitrary-SQL RPC (`exec_sql`)
findings.evidence: `const { error } = await supa.rpc("exec_sql", { sql: sqlText })` and, on failure, the thrown message reads: `Supabase exec_sql RPC missing — add a SECURITY DEFINER function. Underlying: ${error.message}`.
findings.impact: In Postgres, `CREATE FUNCTION` grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC by default, and Supabase exposes every RPC to the `anon`/`authenticated` roles over PostgREST. A `SECURITY DEFINER exec_sql(sql text)` created as instructed and not explicitly revoked is callable by any unauthenticated internet user via `POST /rest/v1/rpc/exec_sql` with an arbitrary `sql` body — total database compromise. The error message is an instruction to build that backdoor.
findings.fix: Never ship a raw-SQL RPC. If the migration runner needs raw SQL on the Supabase fallback, run it out-of-band with the service-role key and delete the `exec_sql` call and the guidance from the error message. If a SQL-execution RPC is unavoidable, revoke it from anon/authenticated, keep it service_role-only, and restrict it to an allowlist of statements.

findings.title: Two data stores with two different security models, selected at runtime by whichever env var happens to be set
findings.evidence: `return process.env.DATABASE_URL || process.env.POSTGRES_URL || process.env.POSTGRES_PRISMA_URL || null` (lib/db/neon.ts:26) — three different names, resolved at runtime, decide which database the app talks to. `getDbLayer()` (lib/backup.ts:168-170) then picks `neonDb` (raw SQL, no RLS) or `supabaseDb` (PostgREST, RLS enforced) for the same operation. The codebase states the asymmetry explicitly: lib/api/with-db-auth.ts:14-16 — 'there's no RLS on Neon, so the application code carries that responsibility' — while the Supabase path relies on the RLS policies in supabase-setup/*.sql.
findings.impact: The same feature has two different guarantees depending on an environment variable. `neonDb.select` (`select * from public.${table} where user_id = $1`) has no RLS behind it, and the Neon connection role is normally the table owner, so enabling RLS later would not apply to it either (no `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` anywhere — verified by grep). A forgotten `user_id` filter is a cross-tenant leak on the Neon path and is silently blocked on the Supabase path, so the bug only reproduces in production.
findings.fix: Pick one primary store explicitly and fail fast if it is not configured (do not silently fall back); enable RLS on Neon with `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` plus per-user policies as the safety net; keep the fallback behind an explicit, loudly-logged feature flag.

findings.title: Password-reset and email-verification redirects are built from a dev-named env var with no origin validation
findings.evidence: `const siteUrl = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DEV_SUPABASE_REDIRECT_URL || (process.env.VERCEL_URL ? `https://${process.env.VERCEL_URL}` : "http://localhost:3000")` then `await supabase.auth.resetPasswordForEmail(email, { redirectTo: `${siteUrl}/auth/reset-password` })`; the sign-up action uses the same expression (lib/actions.ts:74).
findings.impact: If NEXT_PUBLIC_DEV_SUPABASE_REDIRECT_URL is left pointing at a dev or localhost origin in production, every password-reset email sends the recipient a link to the wrong host and the single-use recovery token is delivered to that origin. If neither variable is set the link points at http://localhost:3000. If VERCEL_URL resolves to a preview deployment, the token is handed to that deployment. Any of these either breaks account recovery or leaks a recovery token to an origin that is not the production one.
findings.fix: Derive the redirect origin from a single validated `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` that must be an absolute https:// URL on the production domain, refuse to send a reset email if it is unset or is not the production origin, and register the exact redirect URI in the Supabase dashboard's allow-list.

findings.title: `typescript.ignoreBuildErrors: true` with 54 pre-existing type errors and no CI to catch them
findings.evidence: `typescript: { ignoreBuildErrors: true }` with the comment 'Strict TS, but don't fail builds on unrelated errors. Real errors are caught by tsc in CI.' — but there is no CI in the repository: no `.github/` directory and no workflow YAML anywhere (verified with find). The captured baseline at audit/baseline/tsc-baseline.log shows 54 pre-existing `tsc --noEmit` errors, concentrated in app/api/templates/[id]/preview/route.ts (16), app/dashboard/damages/page.tsx (10) and app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts (6).
findings.impact: Type errors ship silently. The type system is exactly what would catch an auth or tenancy mistake (a handler that forgets to return a NextResponse, a route whose params type does not match, a query whose result shape is wrong), and the stated safety net does not exist. The comment documents a control that was never built.
findings.fix: Clear the 54 errors, drop `ignoreBuildErrors`, and add a CI job that runs `tsc --noEmit` (plus `npm test` and `npm audit`) on every push — the claim in the comment should become true.
findings.fix_notes: The error count is now known and documented (audit/baseline/tsc-baseline.log: 54 at baseline, 52 now) and the count is checked in CI independently of the build. The typescript.ignoreBuildErrors flag is still set, because clearing the remaining errors first is a separate mechanical cleanup.

findings.title: next@16.3.8 is inside the affected range of two critical RCE advisories and one high DoS advisory
findings.evidence: `npm audit` reports `next` at severity critical, affected range `16.0.0 - 16.4.0`: GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw 'Next.js: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in Image Optimization API when SVG files are used' (critical), GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr 'Next.js: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in `use cache` functions returning typed arrays' (critical) and GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r 'Next.js: Denial of Service in App Router using Server Actions' (high). `fixAvailable: true`.
findings.impact: Two of the three paths are accidentally closed in this deployment: `images: { unoptimized: true }` (next.config.mjs:11-13) disables the /_next/image optimizer the SVG RCE needs, and a repository-wide search finds no `use cache` directive, so the typed-array RCE has no reachable sink. The Server Actions DoS is live — the app ships Server Actions at lib/actions.ts:1 and app/(marketing)/auth/forgot-password/action.ts:1 — and an unauthenticated attacker can hammer them. The critical advisories sit in the exact framework the whole app is built on, so the mitigation cannot be relied on indefinitely.
findings.fix: Upgrade next to a patched release (`npm audit fix`, or pin to the latest 16.x above the affected range) and re-run `npm run build`; keep images.unoptimized only while it is needed and re-test the SVG path once the optimizer is re-enabled.
findings.fix_notes: next upgraded from ^16.3.8 to ^16.4.3; package-lock.json and pnpm-lock.yaml were regenerated (the repo pins pnpm@10.34.6 via packageManager, so a stale pnpm lockfile would break a Vercel --frozen-lockfile install). npm audit no longer reports the three advisories.

findings.title: zod@3.25.76 is affected by GHSA-mrhx-c7xc-m3w5 (memory exhaustion on oversized constrained collections)
findings.evidence: `npm audit` reports `zod` at severity high, affected range `<4.6.6`, installed 3.25.76, fix requires `zod@4.6.7` (semver-major). The advisory is 'Zod can exhaust memory while validating oversized constrained collections'. The app validates untrusted request bodies with zod on every public endpoint, including constrained collections such as `z.array(z.string().trim().min(1).max(80)).min(1).max(100)` at app/api/reconciliation/bulk/route.ts:7.
findings.impact: A crafted payload sent to a public endpoint can make the validating function allocate far more memory than the schema implies, which on a Vercel serverless function means an out-of-memory kill (and a bill) — a cheap denial of service on a metered runtime. The upgrade is semver-major, so it must be scheduled rather than hot-patched.
findings.fix: Upgrade to zod@^4.6.7 and re-run the validation tests; until then add an explicit byte-size guard on `await request.json()` at the public endpoints and cap array lengths before parsing.

findings.title: No `vercel.json`: no explicit HTTPS redirect, no cron schedule, no per-function duration limits
findings.lines: 1-45 (no vercel.json in the repository root — `ls vercel.json` → 'No such file or directory'; a repo-wide search finds none)
findings.evidence: Deployment configuration is entirely implicit. There is no `crons[]` entry, while app/api/cron/run/route.ts:9-19 documents the endpoint as the replacement for the missing pg_cron ('schedule it externally') and app/api/migrations/run/route.ts:11-22 relies on a runner. There is also no `redirects()` rule for http:// → https://, no headers override, and no `maxDuration` on the long-running backup routes (app/api/backup/route.ts:18, app/api/backup/auto/route.ts:5, app/api/backup/csv/[table]/route.ts:6 all set `export const runtime = "nodejs"` but no duration).
findings.impact: Two concrete consequences. (1) The lease-expiry, recurring-expense, document-expiry and maintenance-reminder scans never run: nothing in the repository schedules POST /api/cron/run and no external scheduler is configured either, so those features are silently dead while the code claims to be the cron replacement. (2) The backup routes serialise the whole tenant dataset to JSON in one invocation with no duration cap, which will exceed the default function timeout on a large tenant — the request dies mid-export.
findings.fix: Add a vercel.json with a `crons[]` entry for /api/cron/run (Vercel Cron sends `Authorization: Bearer $CRON_SECRET`, which the route already accepts), a `maxDuration` for the backup routes, and an explicit http:// → https:// redirect plus a headers block carrying the CSP and cross-origin headers from INFRA-010/INFRA-011.

findings.title: The backup endpoint returns the entire tenant dataset in one response with no size cap and no Cache-Control: no-store
findings.evidence: `const payload = await exportBackup(userId, email, { tables: body?.tables })` then `NextResponse.json({ ok: true, id, ..., payload: inlinePayload })` (line 92) — the response carries the full contents of up to 20 tables (lib/system.ts:22-42, including user_profiles, paybills, c2b_transactions and reconciliation_audit) as one JSON document. The response sets no cache-control header — contrast app/api/export/route.ts:81, which does set `cache-control: no-store` on the equivalent payload.
findings.impact: A large tenant can push the function past its memory or duration limit, taking the request down with it. And because the response omits `Cache-Control: no-store`, an intermediary CDN or proxy is free to cache a response containing every property, tenant, payment, expense, document and reconciliation row the landlord has — the opposite of what /api/export does for the same data.
findings.fix: Return a manifest (id, label, counts, sizes) instead of the inline payload, serve the payload from private storage through a short-lived signed URL, add `cache-control: no-store, private` to every response that carries tenant data, and cap the export size.

findings.title: Team roles are stored but never enforced anywhere in the authorisation path
findings.evidence: `role: z.enum(["admin", "manager", "agent", "accountant", "viewer"]).default("agent")` is written to `team_members.role` (line 52). A repository-wide search for role checks in the authorisation path finds none: lib/api/index.ts (`withAuth`) establishes only 'a valid session' and 'the caller owns this row' — it never looks at a role, a membership or a company. The only `role` references under app/api/** are this write path.
findings.impact: The role is decorative. A teammate added as `viewer` has exactly the same API access as the workspace owner — they can create a backup, invite further members, connect a paybill and issue an M-Pesa push. A landlord who believes they have limited a contractor's access has granted full access to every property, tenant, payment and document. A role called `admin` grants no additional privilege either, so there is no way to grant privileged access, and no way to revoke it.
findings.fix: Introduce a real authorisation layer: resolve the caller's membership and role for the company that owns the row and check it in withAuth (and in a withDbAuth equivalent) before any write. Until that exists, remove the role field from the UI so it does not promise isolation that is not enforced.

findings.title: No session revocation, no token-lifetime policy, and cookie flags fully delegated to library defaults
findings.evidence: The middleware rebuilds the cookie on every request: `setAll(cookiesToSet) { cookiesToSet.forEach(({ name, value }) => request.cookies.set(name, value)); response = NextResponse.next({ request }); cookiesToSet.forEach(({ name, value, options }) => response.cookies.set(name, value, options)) }`. The `options` — httpOnly, secure, sameSite, maxAge — come entirely from @supabase/ssr's defaults; the application never sets or asserts them and no test pins them. `signOut()` (lib/actions.ts:109-116) revokes the current session only, and there is no 'sign out everywhere' or revoke-all path anywhere in the codebase. No access-token or refresh-token lifetime is configured or asserted (Supabase defaults: 1 h access, 7 d refresh). The marketing cookie policy (app/(marketing)/legal/cookies/page.tsx:35) asserts `sb-*` cookies are 'httponly, secure' — a claim the code does not enforce or test.
findings.impact: A stolen refresh token stays usable for up to a week and the owner cannot invalidate it — there is no revocation list, no 'log out all devices' action and no admin-side session listing. The httpOnly/secure/sameSite posture of the one cookie that grants full access to the landlord's data is decided by a library default nobody here verifies, so a Supabase project-level setting change silently weakens it.
findings.fix: Set and pin the cookie options explicitly when writing the session cookie (`httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax", path: "/"`), add a 'sign out of all devices' action that revokes all refresh tokens for the user, shorten the refresh-token lifetime in the Supabase project, and assert the cookie flags in a test.

findings.title: Two `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` sinks — safe today, unguarded against future user data
findings.evidence: app/layout.tsx:89-103 injects `JSON.stringify({ "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "SoftwareApplication", ... })` into a `<script type="application/ld+json">` — a static object literal, so it is safe. components/ui/chart.tsx:83-95 injects a `<style>` block built from `THEMES` and the chart `config` — also developer-supplied, also safe today. A repository-wide grep for `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` returns exactly these two hits.
findings.impact: No live XSS. The risk is that both are unguarded sinks with no CSP in front of them (INFRA-010) and no `</script>` escaping: if either value ever becomes user- or database-derived (a chart label from a tenant record, a product name), the `JSON.stringify` call does not escape `</script>` and the payload breaks out of the tag. With no CSP that is a direct stored-XSS path to the dashboard.
findings.fix: Keep the sinks but escape `</` as `<\/` inside any JSON embedded in a `<script>` tag, and add a lint rule banning new dangerouslySetInnerHTML uses. With the CSP from INFRA-010 in place, an injected inline script is blocked even if a sink is misused.

findings.title: `images.unoptimized: true` disables the Next.js image pipeline
findings.evidence: `images: { unoptimized: true }` with the comment 'Use Next's own image pipeline. (unoptimized: true disables the proxy and lets images be served straight from the host — ...)' — the comment describes the opposite of what the flag does.
findings.impact: Every renders as a raw : no format negotiation, no responsive srcset, no resizing, and no protection against a decompression bomb or an oversized user upload being served at full resolution (the property-photo route accepts 8 MB images and the public bucket serves them verbatim). This also means the next/image optimizer — the sink for GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw — is off, which is currently the only thing keeping that critical advisory from being reachable.
findings.fix: Turn images.unoptimized back off once next is upgraded past the affected range (the optimizer is the patched, size-limiting path), or enforce an explicit width/height and a server-side re-encode at upload time. Fix the misleading comment either way.

findings.title: POST /api/backup/auto accepts an arbitrary `user_id` in the body
findings.evidence: `const body = (await request.json().catch(() => ({}))) as { user_id?: string; frequency?: "daily" | "weekly" | "monthly" }` and `const due = body.user_id ? candidates.filter((c) => c.userId === body.user_id) : (candidates as any[]).filter((c) => c._due)`; the fallback at lines 84-86 fabricates a candidate for `body.user_id` with no ownership check.
findings.impact: With BACKUP_CRON_SECRET set, the holder of that secret can make the server export and store a full backup for any user id. It is admin-scoped by the secret so the blast radius is small, but the parameter gives the endpoint an unnecessary cross-tenant primitive and the `user_id` is never validated against the set of users that actually have auto_backup enabled.
findings.fix: Remove the `user_id` body parameter and drive selection purely from `user_profiles.auto_backup`; if a manual trigger is needed, expose it as a separate authenticated route that resolves the target from the caller's own session.

findings.title: One static bearer secret grants full schema/DDL control, with no rotation, no request signing and a NODE_ENV-gated dev fallback
findings.evidence: The design note states it plainly: 'The secret header is a soft check; the real security is that this endpoint runs only on the host that owns the database. There is no admin user — anyone with the secret can apply patches.' The check is `if (expected && got === expected) return null` — a single static string, reusable forever, with no timestamp, no nonce, no request signature and no rotation mechanism anywhere in the repo. The dev fallback (`if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production") { ...any signed-in user... }`) is gated on an environment variable rather than an explicit opt-in. applyPatch then runs a file's contents with `sql.unsafe(sqlText)` (app/api/migrations/run/route.ts:113-117) and /api/migrations/rollback does the same (line 80).
findings.impact: A leaked MIGRATION_SECRET — from a CI log, a Vercel environment-variable dump, a screenshot, a shared secret store, a former contractor — is an irrevocable, permanent grant of arbitrary SQL execution against production. It cannot be scoped, cannot be rotated without a coordinated deploy, and cannot be attributed to a caller. Any deployment that is not literally NODE_ENV=production (a self-hosted box, a container image with the default env) silently accepts any signed-in subscriber as a migration admin, and `POST /api/cron/run?migrate=1` runs pending migrations under CRON_SECRET.
findings.fix: Treat the migration endpoints as a privileged operation with a real identity: require a short-lived signed token (HMAC over method + path + timestamp + nonce) issued by a CLI, and reject requests older than a few minutes. Gate the dev fallback on an explicit ALLOW_DEV_ADMIN=1 opt-in instead of NODE_ENV !== "production", and make the cron/migration paths require the secret even in development. Rotate MIGRATION_SECRET on a schedule and keep it out of shared logs.

findings.title: No user-supplied URL is ever fetched — but /api/geocode is an unthrottled open relay to a third-party geocoder
findings.evidence: Every server-side fetch in the codebase targets a hard-coded host: `https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search?...` (app/api/geocode/route.ts:8, app/api/properties/[id]/geocode/route.ts:14 and 37-44), the Daraja API (lib/mpesa/daraja.ts:78, 172, 218, 368, 496), and the Stripe SDK. No route accepts a `url` / `imageUrl` / `src` parameter to fetch; there is no image proxy. The user-controlled input is only interpolated into the query string of a fixed host — `q=${encodeURIComponent(search)}` (line 8) — correctly encoded, so there is no SSRF and no private-IP reachability here. What the route does have is no throttling: it will proxy a request to Nominatim for every caller.
findings.impact: Not SSRF, but a third-party abuse and availability problem: the OpenStreetMap Foundation's usage policy requires at most 1 request/second and a meaningful User-Agent, so an unthrottled relay gets the app's egress IP (and possibly the Vercel shared-IP range) blocked, which breaks geocoding for every tenant. It is also a free bandwidth/latency amplifier aimed at a third party, and the responses are cached with `next: { revalidate: 3600 }`, so a burst can poison the cache for an hour.
findings.fix: Add a per-user and per-IP rate limit and a server-side cache to /api/geocode, require authentication, and set a compliant User-Agent that includes a contact address (NOMINATIM_EMAIL is already read at app/api/properties/[id]/geocode/route.ts:41 but is not applied to the public route).

findings.title: The migration runner silently discards every statement that follows a comment block
findings.evidence: The runner split a file on /;\s*$/m and then filtered out every chunk whose first characters were '--'. A chunk that began with a comment — but also contained a real statement — was discarded whole. Measured against this repo's own migrations: 001-core.sql lost 9 of 25 chunks (including every create table), 002-support.sql lost 10, 004-marketing-forms.sql lost 8, 005-encryption.sql lost 3 (including the blind-index alter table statements). The runner then failed on the surviving create index statements with 'column does not exist', leaving the schema half-migrated.
findings.impact: npm run db:migrate — the command the runbook tells the owner to run — does not apply the schema. A deployment that appeared to migrate successfully would be missing tables and columns, and the failure would surface at runtime as a missing-table error that the application swallows.
findings.fix: Replaced with a comment-aware splitter (splitSqlStatements in lib/db/migrate.ts): -- comments are stripped rather than discarding the statement that followed them, a semicolon inside a single-quoted string does not end a statement, and a dollar-quoted (2309 ... 2309) body is kept intact. lib/db/migrate.test.ts pins the behaviour and asserts that every statement of every migration file survives.
findings.fix_notes: lib/db/migrate.ts now exports splitSqlStatements(). 005-encryption.sql applies all 8 statements; 001-core.sql keeps its create table statements; the plpgsql function bodies in 002-support.sql arrive whole instead of in fragments.
